The first year, I grated potatoes, chopped onions, and watched. The second year, I fed everything but the eggs into the machine and announced that I would make the latkes—and I did. My mounting pile of crisp delights was carried to the feast by the wife who baffled me: our books closed, our banter hushed, money rendered useless in the apartment—house, my in-laws called it—with its new-wave thump at one end and its haze of ganja at the other, the very rooms in which she had once knelt to tell the no one who listened *no more, no, no more, no*, a three-year-old mouthing the essential prayer.

The uncle, made rich by a single song, stacked three latkes high and dug in, holding forth on critics and Koch—everyone crunching now, slathering applesauce, slurping tea—on Rabin and Mehitabel, on radio and Durrell, on how a song is either a poem or it is no song at all, and the reverse besides. Finished, he leveled a greasy finger at me and declared, "You can't be a goy. You"—and I repeat it for all to hear—"are an honorary Jew!" An impossible dream, and yet one my latkes honored for five more years.

Then came the wailing. Then the dust.

# The Latke Maker

Over the years, my role in the family feast transformed slowly but completely. At first, I was content simply to watch—observing the careful rituals of the kitchen, offering my hands only for the humblest of tasks. I peeled and I grated, I fetched and I stirred, learning by proximity the choreography of the meal. But gradually, season by season, I earned my place at the stove itself, until one year I realized I had taken full ownership of the latkes. They were mine to make now, my responsibility and my offering to the gathering.

The apartment itself was a vessel of layered histories, thick with contrasts that lived side by side. Music drifted through the rooms, mingling with the sweet haze of marijuana smoke, while somewhere beneath the warmth and celebration lingered something older and more painful. I came to know the story of my wife as a small girl, kneeling in prayer against some loss she could not yet name—a child bargaining with heaven, hoping to hold on to something already slipping away. The walls seemed to hold both the laughter and the grief, refusing to let either one go.

When the family gathered, the feast came alive. It was a loud and communal affair, filled with the clatter of plates and the passing of dishes, the constant motion of people eating and talking over one another. Conversation ranged freely across every subject—the threads of cultural memory, the heat of political debate, arguments about music and literature that rose and fell like tides. It was a household that loved to argue as much as it loved to eat, and the two appetites fed each other.

It was at one such gathering that the uncle bestowed upon me the highest honor he could imagine. Raising his voice above the din, he declared me an "honorary Jew"—a moment of acceptance that folded me into the family and its long inheritance. My latkes, crisp and golden, upheld that title for several years afterward, a small annual proof that I belonged.

But nothing holds forever. The poem closes on a note of quiet finality, the warmth of those crowded rooms giving way at last to loss. Whatever bound me to that family—the marriage, the shared table, the honorary belonging—eventually dissolved, leaving behind only grief and an emptiness where the feast had been.

# On Being an Honorary Jew

The poem opens in a kitchen thick with the smell of frying oil, where the speaker stands year after year at the stove, learning the particular art of making latkes. This is his role, the task assigned to him at the annual holiday feast, and through its repetition the ritual becomes something more than cooking. Each grated potato, each spattering pan, marks his slow initiation into a family not born to him but chosen through marriage. His wife's Jewish family becomes the world he steps into once a year, and the latkes are his offering, his ticket of entry, the labor that earns him a place at the crowded table.

The gatherings themselves come alive with noise and argument. The speaker captures the boisterous intellectual banter that fills the room—debates over politics and scripture, jokes told over one another, voices rising in the particular music of a family that loves to argue as a form of affection. There is warmth beneath the clamor, a generosity that folds the outsider in. He, the gentile son-in-law from another tradition, finds himself not merely tolerated but embraced, drawn into the current of talk and laughter that runs through these rooms.

At the center of the poem stands the uncle, a figure of authority and humor, who one year makes his pronouncement: the speaker is henceforth an "honorary Jew." It is said half in jest and wholly in earnest, a blessing and a welcome delivered with a flourish. In that moment the years of latke-making, of listening and belonging, are ratified. The uncle names what has quietly become true. The speaker is one of them now, accepted into the lineage of memory and meal.

But the poem does not let this belonging rest untroubled. The declaration is dated, marked in time, and the speaker tells us it lasted only five more years. After that came the wailing and the dust—the language of Jewish mourning, the torn cloth and the covered mirrors, the return of the body to the earth. Loss enters the poem and ends the season of gatherings. The uncle, or others who made those feasts possible, are gone, and with them the ritual that held the family together in that particular form.

What remains is the ache of understanding. The five years of being an honorary Jew were precious precisely because they could not last. The poem closes on the fragility of familial connection—how quickly the boisterous table falls silent, how the warmth of belonging is shadowed always by the certainty of loss. The latkes, the banter, the uncle's generous naming: all of it was a gift held only for a while, made more luminous by its ending.

# Pioneers of Their Fields: Koch and Rabin

Throughout history, certain individuals have left an indelible mark on science and society. Among the names that continue to resonate across different disciplines are Koch and Rabin—two surnames associated with groundbreaking contributions to the modern world.

## The Legacy of Robert Koch

Robert Koch stands as one of the founding figures of modern bacteriology. Working in the late nineteenth century, the German physician and microbiologist identified the specific bacteria responsible for anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera. His development of "Koch's postulates"—a set of criteria used to establish a causal relationship between a microbe and a disease—transformed the way medicine understood infection. For his work on tuberculosis, Koch was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905, cementing his status as a giant of the biological sciences.

## The Contributions of Rabin

The name Rabin carries significance in more than one arena. In computer science, Michael O. Rabin is celebrated for his pioneering work in algorithms and computational theory. Together with Dana Scott, he received the Turing Award for foundational contributions to the theory of automata. Rabin is also known for probabilistic algorithms, including methods for primality testing that remain influential in cryptography and data security today.

In a different sphere, Yitzhak Rabin served as Prime Minister of Israel and became a central figure in efforts to achieve peace in the Middle East, an endeavor for which he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

## The Enduring Influence

What unites the names Koch and Rabin is the way each has shaped the trajectory of human knowledge and progress. Whether through the microscope, the mathematical proof, or the negotiating table, these figures remind us that dedicated inquiry and bold thinking can change the course of history. Their legacies continue to inspire new generations of scientists, thinkers, and leaders around the globe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a non-Jewish man who marries into a Jewish family and, over years of Hanukkah celebrations, learns to make latkes—capturing the warmth, the eccentric relatives, and the eventual loss when the marriage ends.
counterfactuals.output:
**Learning Latkes**

The first year I stood in the doorway
of a kitchen that was not my inheritance,
watching your mother grate potatoes
with the ferocity of someone
who had survived things she would not name.

*Not like that,* she said,
taking the box grater from my hands,
and I understood I was being taught
something older than the recipe—
how to belong to a table
that had set a place for me
before I knew I wanted it.

The years learned their own rhythm.
Uncle Sol arguing politics with the wall.
Your aunt who kissed both my cheeks
and left lipstick like a benediction.
The cousins multiplying,
the menorah crowding with candles,
oil spitting in the pan like applause.

By the fifth December
I could feel doneness in my wrist—
the exact gold, the edges crisp as autumn,
the way your grandmother's hands must have known it
in a country that no longer exists.
You'd come up behind me at the stove,
press your face between my shoulder blades,
and I'd think: *this. This is the whole of it.*

I never converted. I only converted
the way winter light converts a room,
the way I learned to say the blessings
by their shape in your mouth,
the way the applesauce and sour cream
became a small liturgy
I could perform by heart.

Now the pan hangs in a different kitchen.
December comes anyway,
indifferent as always,
and I find I still know the trick of it—
how to keep the oil from turning bitter,
how much to make for a family
that is no longer mine to feed.

I grate the potatoes alone.
The old knowledge stays in the wrist
even after the hand that taught it
lets go.

And your mother—
I heard she asks about me sometimes,
which is its own kind of candle,
lit and lit and lit
against a dark that always wins by morning,
and always, always
we light it again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem told in the first person, tracing several years of an annual family gathering through the ritual of frying potato pancakes, ending on a note of grief with the phrases "Then the wailing. Then the dust."
counterfactuals.output:
Latkes

I

The first year I remember standing small,
my chin just level with the counter's edge,
watching Grandmother's knuckles work the block
of yellow soap-hard potatoes into snow.
The grater bit. The bowl filled up with white
that browned like apples left too long in air.
She said, *You do not stop for that. You fry.*
And oil spat gold across the kitchen tile.
We ate them standing, burning our fingers,
and she laughed at us, and we did not mind.

II

The second year my mother took the grater.
Grandmother sat, directing from her chair—
*More egg. Less flour. The oil is not yet ready;
wait until the bread crumb dances in it.*
I dropped a match of onion in the pan
and learned the difference between smoke and steam.
The house filled up with cousins, coats, and cold,
and someone's baby cried, and someone sang,
and Grandmother ate one and closed her eyes
as if the taste were somewhere far behind her.

III

The years ran on like oil across a plate.
I grew into the grater. My own knuckles
learned the ache, the rhythm, and the risk.
Grandmother's hands went quiet in her lap,
translucent as the skins we peeled away.
She still could tell by sound if we were ready—
*Not yet,* she'd say, before the oil was hot,
her ears still keeping vigil where her eyes
had started their slow surrender to the dark.
We plated them. She ate them, one, then none.

IV

The last year that she came, she did not speak
of egg or flour or when the oil was ready.
She sat beside the window, wrapped in wool,
and watched the snow do what the graters do,
reducing the wide world to something white.
I brought her one. She held it, did not eat.
*You've got it now,* she said. That was the blessing.
The kitchen roared with all the living noise—
the cousins, coats, and cold, the singing, steam—
and she was quiet at the center of it.

V

This year I grate alone before they come.
The bowl fills up with snow that browns like time.
I drop the batter, and the oil says *yes*
in the old language only oil can speak.
I plate them. Set one at the empty chair.
The window holds the snow. The snow holds nothing.
And for a moment I can almost hear
her voice correcting me across the years—
*Not yet,* it says. *Not yet.* And then the hush.
Then the wailing. Then the dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about being called an "honorary Jew" by a family member at a holiday meal, weaving together food, music, arguing about critics and politics, and the memory of a failed marriage.
counterfactuals.output:
Honorary Jew

The brisket came apart beneath my fork
the way things do when they've been cooked with time,
and Uncle Saul, three glasses into pork-
forbidden wine, declared me half-divine—

*an honorary Jew*, he said, and laughed,
and passed the horseradish that made me cry
in ways that had no sorrow in them. Draft
of Klezmer from the kitchen radio, a high

clarinet unspooling like an argument
none of us would win: whether the Times
was right about that play, whether they meant
to bury it, whether the critic's crimes

were worse than the playwright's. Someone brought up Gaza.
Someone brought up rent, the mayor, God.
My ex once said I couldn't hold a *pause a*
moment—always answering, the flawed

habit of a man who fears the quiet.
She was raised in this, the loving noise,
the table as a small permitted riot,
and I, the goy who envied all their poise

at grief and joy at once. We'd split the year
her mother died, the same December week
I learned to say *l'chaim* without fear
of getting it wrong, the vowels going weak

against my Midwest tongue. And here I sit,
still folded in, though she has moved to Maine,
still handed plates, still asked to argue, fit
for adoption by the ache and the champagne.

*Honorary*—meaning: not by blood,
but by the willingness to stay and eat,
to let the music rise above the flood
of politics, to find the bitter sweet,

to be the one they keep a chair beside
though the marriage that first brought me failed and fell.
The candles gutter. Saul has teared and sighed.
I pass the wine. I've learned to argue well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a densely packed, image-rich poem about latkes and belonging—include a bohemian apartment with clashing music, a child praying "no more," an uncle who got rich from a song, and a bittersweet ending about divorce.
counterfactuals.output:
# Oil and Belonging

The latkes hiss in a pan that's older than the marriage
now dissolving in the next room, potato-shredded knuckles
bleeding faith into the batter, onion tears indistinguishable
from the real ones. This is the bohemian apartment where
Coltrane wars with klezmer wars with the neighbor's bass
that thumps like a second, disagreeing heart—

three musics, no harmony, and yet
we gather. We always gather here,
among the tapestries thumbtacked crooked to the wall,
the incense fighting frying oil, the paperback Kabbalah
splayed beside a Buddha someone bought in Prague.

My cousin, small and folded on the floor,
prays *no more, no more,* not to God
but to the platter growing like a golden accusation—
her stomach a democracy already overthrown,
her mouth a treaty broken by the next crisp coin of oil.

And Uncle Saul arrives late, always late,
who wrote one song in nineteen-eighty-something,
a jingle, really, but the royalties still bloom—
he wears the wealth like cologne, too much,
and tips the delivery boy in stories.
*I made my fortune on a hook,* he laughs,
*eleven notes and a rhyme about detergent,*
and no one knows if he is bragging or in mourning.

We eat. We are a people who have learned
to salt our joy with knowing it will end.
The sour cream, the applesauce—the ancient argument
of which belongs—goes on, will always go on,
a debate more permanent than love.

Because in the next room the papers wait,
two signatures apart from a family
becoming a diaspora of one address into two.
The latkes will be split. The menorah. The dog.
The way she laughed when he burned the first batch
is already becoming *the way she used to laugh.*

Still—
we press the potatoes into shape.
We fry the shapeless into something that will hold
for just a moment, golden, hot, and whole,
before the oil forgets it, before the plate is cleared,
before the child's small prayer is answered
by the simple, terrible mercy of the food running out.

This is belonging: the crowded, clashing kitchen,
the uncle rich in one bright note of loss,
the marriage frying down to its last crisp edge—
and all of us, still here, still hungry,
still passing the plate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a confessional free-verse piece that moves year by year, starting with a newcomer grating potatoes and watching, building to acceptance at the feast, then collapsing into the aftermath of a broken marriage.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Latkes Knew

**Year One**

I grate the potatoes wrong—
too coarse, your mother says,
not unkindly, taking the box grater
from my raw and reddened hands.

I am the new one here,
the girl who married in,
who does not know the prayers
by heart, who mouths them
half a beat behind.

I watch the oil.
I watch your family
laugh in a language
of old kitchens.
I am learning
which drawer holds the forks.

---

**Year Three**

My knuckles remember now.
I bleed less.
I know to squeeze the shredded white
in cheesecloth, wring the water out,
that the secret is the dryness,
the patience of the wringing.

You touch my back
as you reach past me for the salt.
Small thing. I keep it.

---

**Year Five**

Your mother lets me lead the blessing.
*Baruch atah*—
and I do not stumble.

The children—ours now,
two of them, flour on their cheeks—
stand on chairs to watch the oil bloom gold.

At the table I am not
married in.
I am simply *in.*
The applesauce is mine.
They ask for it by name.

I have arrived
the way a river arrives:
slowly, then all at once,
then like it was always
going to be here.

---

**Year Eight**

The recipe is muscle now.
I could make it blind.

Which is good,
because I am not looking at you anymore
and you are not looking at me.

We pass the platter
across a silence
the children fill with noise,
thank God for the noise.

Your mother watches us
the way she watched me once—
learning something,
half a beat behind.

---

**Year Ten**

I grate the potatoes alone.

Half the recipe.
I keep making the whole thing
and throwing the rest away
because my hands
don't know the smaller number.

The box grater is mine now—
the divorce was generous
in its small cruelties,
you did not fight me for the kitchen.

I mouth the blessing
to an empty room,
half a beat behind
the woman I used to be,
the one who wrung the water out
and thought the dryness
would keep everything
from falling apart.

The oil still blooms.
The children come on Tuesdays.

I have learned the smaller number
by heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
